newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnia local polls by end-November - Solana.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia local polls by end-November - Solana.

text.p: NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana said on Thursday he expected municipal elections in Bosnia to take place before the end of November and he vowed NATO would provide the necessary security umbrella for them.
"The municipal election will probably take place before the end of the month of November," Solana told reporters during an informal NATO defence ministers' meeting in Bergen.

Solana stressed the decision was a matter for the poll organisers, the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), but said after recent briefings from OSCE officials he now expected the poll to go ahead.

The OSCE has come under intense pressure to hold the poll in November to allow NATO's plans to withdraw its force by the end of the year to begin on schedule. The alliance has promised not to begin "draw-down" before the municipal polls are held.

Solana said NATO's 52,000-strong Implementation Force (IFOR) in Bosnia would keep open 19 agreed routes to allow refugees to cross ethnic boundary lines to vote in areas from which they were forced to flee.
He said the alliance expected thousands of people to cross to vote in their former home districts would make the policing of the poll more difficult than countrywide elections earlier this month.
NATO ministers agreed on Wednesday they would probably have to keep thousands of troops in Bosnia next year after the mandate of the current peace mission expires on December 20.
It was the first public acknowledgement by the alliance that such a force may be necessary.
Officials said they had agreed to order the military to draw up a number of options for a possible follow-on to IFOR, Europe's biggest military deployment since World War Two.
"We see the basis of a consensus for a new mission emerging," German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe told reporters. He said any new mission would involve "deterrence and stabilisation".
NATO sources said that although U.S. Defence Secretary William Perry did not explicitly say U.S. troops would be in the force, there was broad agreement it would include the same countries as IFOR.

The United States currently has some 15,000 troops in the IFOR force, sent in last December to police the Dayton peace accords. Britain and France, the other main contributors, will not remain without a U.S. ground presence.
The issue is highly sensitive in the United States ahead of November's presidential elections. President Bill Clinton originally said the troops would be home by the end of the year.
